software-developer.intro: Learn software development from first principles. Write code, debug it, ship it, and work with other developers — the skills that turn an idea into working software.

skillDomains.name: Programming Fundamentals
skillDomains.description: The core building blocks of code — the grammar you'll use every day.

skills.name: Variables & Data Types
skills.description: Store and manipulate values: numbers, text, true/false, and collections.

modules.title: What code actually is
modules.content:
Code is a set of instructions. A computer does exactly what you tell it — nothing more, nothing less. Your job is to be precise.

Every program, from a mobile wallet to a banking system, is built from a few small pieces:

  • Variables — named boxes that hold values
  • Types — the kind of value in the box (number, text, true/false)
  • Operations — what you can do with those values

That's it. Everything else is combining these in clever ways.

modules.title: The three types you'll use forever
modules.content:
Numbers

Whole numbers (5), decimals (3.14). Used for counts, prices, calculations.

Strings

Text, in quotes ("Hello"). Used for names, messages, everything written.

Booleans

Only true or false. Used for decisions.

Master these three and you can write 80% of any program. The rest is variation.

steps.q: You need to store a user's name. Which type?
You need to store whether a user has paid. Which type?
steps.f: Yes/no state is boolean — true or false.

steps.q: You need to store the price of an item. Which type?
steps.f: Prices are numbers, and usually decimals.

modules.title: Name your variables well
modules.prompt: You're writing code for a school to track student fees. List at least 6 variables you would need and choose a name for each. Explain why you chose each name.
modules.context: Good variable names make code readable. Bad names cause bugs six months later.
rubric: Uses descriptive names (not x, y, temp)
Follows consistent naming convention (camelCase or snake_case)
Distinguishes between similar concepts (feeTotal vs feePaid)
Avoids abbreviations that aren't universally understood
Every name reads clearly out of context

modules.title: Model a real-world system
modules.prompt: Pick a real West African business (a market stall, a mobile money kiosk, a tailoring shop). Write a one-page document that identifies at least 10 variables the business would need to track and assigns each a data type.
steps: Choose a real business you know
List every piece of information the owner tracks
Assign a type to each (number, string, boolean)
Group related variables together
Write a one-paragraph reflection on what you learned

skills.name: Control Flow
skills.description: Make the program take different paths based on conditions, and repeat work.

modules.title: If this, then that
modules.content:
Programs make decisions with if statements:

IF the user's balance is greater than the price → allow the purchase.
ELSE → show "insufficient funds".

Real programs have nested decisions:

IF balance > price:
  IF account not frozen:
    allow purchase
  ELSE:
    show "account frozen"
ELSE:
  show "insufficient funds"

Every branching business rule becomes an if/else chain.

modules.title: Loops — do it again
modules.content:
Loops repeat work. Two common kinds:

For loop

Runs a known number of times. "For each student in the list, print their name."

While loop

Runs until a condition changes. "While the user hasn't pressed 'exit', keep showing the menu."

Loops are what make computers fast. A human prints 10 names slowly. A loop prints a million in a second.

steps.q: if age >= 18 then 'adult' else 'minor' — what does this return for age = 15?
steps.f: 15 is not >= 18, so the else branch runs: 'minor'.

steps.q: A loop for i = 1 to 3: print(i) — what gets printed?
while balance > 0: withdraw(10) with balance starting at 25 — how many withdrawals?

modules.title: Write a pricing rule
modules.prompt: A mobile money agent charges 1% of any transaction over 100 Le, with a minimum fee of 2 Le. Write the logic in plain English (not code) as a series of IF/ELSE statements.
modules.context: Turning business rules into precise logic is 70% of programming.

modules.title: Document a real business process
modules.prompt: Choose a real process (school registration, market stall pricing, mobile money transfer). Draw a flowchart showing the decisions and loops involved.
steps: Pick a process you've observed
Draw boxes for actions and diamonds for decisions
Show at least 2 decision points
Show at least 1 loop
Write a short explanation

skills.name: Functions
skills.description: Package logic into reusable pieces with clear names.

modules.title: Functions — named blocks of logic
modules.content:
A function is a named box of code you can call by name:

calculateTax(income) → returns the tax owed

Functions take inputs (parameters) and return outputs.

Benefits:

  • Write once, use many times
  • Test in isolation
  • Give meaningful names to complex logic
  • Reuse across the whole project

Great code is a collection of small, well-named functions.

steps.q: Which is the best function to extract from a payment system?
steps.f: Clear name, clear inputs. Single responsibility.

steps.q: Which of these is a good function name?
steps.f: Descriptive names tell the reader what the function does.

steps.q: A function that does five unrelated things is:

modules.title: Design a function signature
modules.prompt: You're building a school report card system. Design a function called generateReport that takes a student's data and returns a formatted report. Describe what inputs it needs and what it returns.
modules.context: Function design is about inputs, outputs, and clarity.
modules.placeholder:
Function name: generateReport
Inputs: …
Outputs: …
What it does: …
rubric: Lists all necessary inputs (name, grades, attendance)
Avoids side effects (function should only produce the report)
Considers edge cases (missing grades, empty student)

modules.title: Design a small function library
modules.prompt: Choose a domain (a small business, a school, a market stall). Design 8 functions that would be needed to run it. For each, write: the name, the inputs, the output, and one sentence on what it does.
steps: List 8 discrete tasks the domain needs
Design one function per task
Keep each function focused on one job
Ensure inputs and outputs are clear
Order them by when they'd be called

skillDomains.name: Problem Solving
skillDomains.description: The intellectual core of programming — reading, debugging, and designing solutions.

skills.name: Debugging
skills.description: Find out why code isn't doing what you expected.

modules.title: Debugging is a science
modules.content:
Bugs are not mysteries. They are hypotheses waiting to be tested.

The debugging loop

  1. Reproduce — can you make the bug happen reliably?
  2. Read the error — what line, what message?
  3. Form a hypothesis — what do you think is wrong?
  4. Test — add logging or change one thing.
  5. Repeat until fixed.

Bad debuggers change many things at once. Good debuggers change one thing at a time and observe.

steps.q: An app crashes when a user enters their name as "O'Brien". Most likely cause?
o: The apostrophe breaks a string or query
steps.f: Apostrophes in user input break strings and SQL if not escaped.

steps.q: A payment system shows the wrong balance only when two transactions happen at once. What's likely?
o: Race condition — two threads updating without locking
steps.f: Concurrent updates without locking produce race conditions.

steps.q: A webpage works on your laptop but not on your phone. First thing to check?
steps.f: Always suspect the simplest difference first.

modules.title: Debug a broken process
modules.prompt: A school's online registration system is double-charging parents who click the 'pay' button twice. Write a step-by-step plan to fix this — how would you reproduce it, what would you check, and what would you change?
modules.context: Double-charging is a critical bug — money is involved.
rubric: Reproduces the bug (click pay twice quickly)
Identifies the likely cause (no button lock after first click)
Proposes disabling the button after first click
Also proposes server-side idempotency (belt and braces)
Considers testing the fix before deploying

skills.name: Algorithm Design
skills.description: Solve problems step by step, at scale.

modules.title: An algorithm is a recipe
modules.content:
An algorithm is a precise sequence of steps to solve a problem. It doesn't have to be code yet — plain English is fine.

Sorting a list of names

  1. Compare first two names. Swap if out of order.
  2. Move to the next pair. Repeat.
  3. When you reach the end, start over.
  4. Stop when a full pass has no swaps.

That's bubble sort — one of hundreds of sorting algorithms.

modules.title: Design a search algorithm
modules.prompt: You have a list of 1,000 students sorted by name. You need to find a specific student quickly. Describe an algorithm — in plain English — that finds them without checking all 1,000 names one by one.
modules.context: Binary search is the answer. Explaining it in plain English is the test of understanding.
rubric: Decides whether to search left or right half
Stops when the item is found or the range is empty
Notes that the list must be sorted for this to work

modules.title: Document three algorithms
modules.prompt: Write plain-English algorithms for three real tasks: (1) finding the largest number in a list, (2) checking if a word is a palindrome, (3) counting how many times each name appears in a class list.
steps: Write each algorithm in numbered steps
Show a worked example with sample data
Note edge cases
Write a one-line summary of each

skillDomains.name: Tools & Workflow
skillDomains.description: The professional toolkit — version control, testing, deployment.

skills.name: Version Control
skills.description: Track every change, collaborate safely, roll back mistakes.

modules.title: Why Git exists
modules.content:
Before version control, developers saved files as project_v1.js, project_final.js, project_final_FINAL.js. It was chaos.

Git solves this. It records every change with:

  • What changed
  • Who changed it
  • When
  • Why (in a message)

You can roll back to any point. Two developers can work on the same file without overwriting each other. Nothing is ever truly lost.

steps.q: You've made changes and want to save them locally with a message. What command?
steps.f: Commit saves locally with a message. Push sends to remote.

steps.q: You want to download the latest changes from the remote repository. What command?
steps.f: git pull fetches and merges remote changes.

steps.q: You've accidentally deleted a file and want to restore it. Where do you look?
o: Git history — the file was committed
steps.f: If the file was committed, git checkout can restore it.

modules.title: Handle a merge conflict
modules.prompt: You and another developer both edited the same file. When you pull, Git shows a merge conflict. Describe what happened and how you would resolve it without losing either person's work.
modules.context: Merge conflicts are normal in team projects.
modules.placeholder:
What happened: …
How I'd resolve it: …
rubric: Explains that both developers edited the same lines
Opens the conflicted file to see the markers
Decides with the other developer which version is correct (or combines them)
Talks to the other developer to prevent future conflicts

skills.name: Testing
skills.description: Prove your code works — and keeps working after changes.

modules.title: Why we test
modules.content:
Code that works today can break tomorrow when someone else changes something. Tests are code that checks other code.

Three kinds of tests

  • Unit tests — test one function in isolation
  • Integration tests — test how functions work together
  • End-to-end tests — test the whole system as a user would use it

You don't need all three on day one. But serious code has at least unit tests.

modules.title: Write tests for a calculator
modules.prompt: You've written a function add(a, b) that returns the sum of two numbers. Write at least 5 test cases you would run to be confident it works.
modules.context: Good tests cover normal cases, edge cases, and unusual inputs.

skillDomains.name: Professional Practice
skillDomains.description: How to work on real teams, on real projects, with real clients.

skills.name: Working with Requirements
skills.description: Turn a vague client request into a precise plan.

modules.title: Clients speak in wishes. You speak in specifics.
modules.content:
A client says: "I want an app for my restaurant."

That's a wish, not a requirement. Your job is to ask until you have specifics:

  • What should the app do? (menu, orders, reservations, all three?)
  • Who uses it? (customers, staff, both?)
  • What's the deadline?
  • What's the budget?
  • What does success look like?

The cost of vague requirements is a project that gets built, then rejected.

modules.title: Clarify a vague brief
modules.prompt: A client says: "I want an app so my market stall can accept mobile money." Write 8 specific questions you would ask before starting.
modules.context: Every question you don't ask now becomes a change request later.
rubric: Asks about payment providers (MTN, Orange, Airtel)
Asks about devices the stall will use

skills.name: Code Review
skills.description: Give and receive feedback on code without ego.

modules.title: Code review is how teams get better
modules.content:
Code review = one developer reads another's code before it's merged. The goal is better code and shared knowledge, not to prove who is smarter.

Rules for giving review

  • Comment on the code, not the person
  • Ask questions instead of making statements
  • Praise good solutions
  • Distinguish 'must fix' from 'nice to have'

Rules for receiving review

  • The code is not you. Critique of code is not critique of you.
  • Ask for clarification if a comment is unclear
  • Thank reviewers — they spent their time helping you

modules.title: Write a code review
modules.prompt: Choose any small piece of code you've written. Write a review of it as if you were another developer. Include 3 things done well and 3 things to improve.
steps: Print or display the code
List what works well
List what could be clearer, faster, or safer
Write the review in a professional tone
Reflect on what you'd do differently next time
